mcqs.question: In the naive Union-Find implementation (no rank, no path compression), what causes find to degrade to O(n) in the worst case?
options: The parent array is stored in the wrong data structure
find() is implemented recursively instead of iteratively
A sequence of unions with no balancing rule can produce a long chain of parent pointers, forcing find to walk the entire chain
The union operation compares element values instead of indices
mcqs.explanation: Without any rule governing which root gets attached under which, a poorly-ordered sequence of unions can chain elements one after another, turning find into a walk no better than traversing a linked list — genuinely O(n) in the worst case. This isn't about the data structure choice or recursion style, and comparing values versus indices is irrelevant to the underlying imbalance problem.

mcqs.question: With union by rank, when does attaching one tree under another's root actually increase the resulting tree's height?
options: Every single time a union operation is performed
Only when the two trees being merged have exactly the same rank/height
Only when the smaller tree has more than 10 nodes
Height increases are entirely random and cannot be bounded
mcqs.explanation: When trees of different heights merge, attaching the shorter one under the taller one's root keeps the taller tree's height unchanged — only when both trees are equally tall does the merge push the height up by exactly one level. This is precisely why the tree's height only grows logarithmically across a whole sequence of unions rather than growing with every single merge.

mcqs.question: The recursive find implementation sets self.parent[x] = self.find(self.parent[x]) before returning. What does this line accomplish beyond finding the root?
options: It deletes the original parent pointer entirely, leaving x disconnected
It recomputes the rank of every ancestor node along the path
It repoints x (and, through the recursion, every ancestor visited) directly to the root, so future find calls on any of them are O(1)
It swaps x with its parent to rebalance the tree by size
mcqs.explanation: Because the recursive call resolves all the way to the root before any assignment happens, every node along the original path gets reassigned to point directly at the root — this is path compression, and it's what makes subsequent finds on those nodes O(1). It doesn't touch rank values, doesn't disconnect x, and doesn't perform any swapping — only repointing.

mcqs.question: Why is Union-Find with union by rank and path compression described as 'almost O(1)' rather than truly O(1)?
options: The true amortized bound is O(the inverse Ackermann function of n), which grows so slowly it's effectively constant for any realistic n, but is not technically a fixed constant
It actually is exactly O(1), and 'almost' is just an informal way of describing it
The bound depends on whether the elements are integers or strings
It's O(log n), which people round down to 'almost constant' informally
mcqs.explanation: The precise amortized bound is O(alpha(n)), the inverse Ackermann function, which grows so slowly that it never exceeds about 5 for any n that could physically exist — but it is a genuine function of n, not a true constant, which is why the honest description is 'almost' rather than exactly O(1). The bound doesn't depend on element type, and O(log n) describes the rank-only optimization without path compression, not the combined result.

mcqs.question: You're building an undirected graph edge by edge and want to detect a cycle as soon as one would be created. How does Union-Find help?
options: Before unioning two nodes for an edge, check if find(a) == find(b) — if they're already in the same set, this edge would close a cycle
Union-Find can only detect cycles in directed graphs, not undirected ones
Run a separate DFS after every edge addition to check for cycles
Cycles can only be detected once the entire graph has been fully built
mcqs.explanation: If two nodes are already in the same set, they're already connected through some existing path — adding a direct edge between them would create a cycle, which is exactly what a same-set check before unioning detects in near-O(1) time. This works specifically well for undirected cycle detection, doesn't require a full DFS per edge, and can flag a cycle immediately rather than waiting for the whole graph to be built.

mcqs.question: An implementation of union by rank always attaches the higher-ranked tree under the lower-ranked tree's root, backwards from the standard rule. What's the consequence?
options: The union operation will throw a runtime error
The sets are merged incorrectly, producing wrong 'same group' answers
There is no consequence, since the rule direction doesn't matter as long as it's applied consistently
The optimization is silently defeated — resulting trees can grow taller than necessary, degrading find back toward the naive O(n) worst case on adversarial sequences
mcqs.explanation: The sets themselves still end up correctly merged either way, so the bug doesn't cause wrong connectivity answers — but attaching the taller tree under the shorter one grows height unnecessarily on every such merge, silently reintroducing the imbalance the optimization exists to prevent. There's no crash, and the direction absolutely matters for keeping trees shallow.
